dataset.name: Daily evapotranspiration changes during heatwaves at 32 NEON sites, 2019-2021
description: This dataset provides partitioned evapotranspiration (ET, the combined loss of water from soil and plant surfaces) anomalies during heatwave events—soil evaporation (E) and transpiration (T)—for 268 heatwave events across 32 National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON) flux sites in the contiguous United States from 2019–2021. Using an ensemble of four high-frequency turbulence methods (Flux-variance Similarity, Conditional Eddy Covariance [CEC], CEC with Water-Use Efficiency, and Conditional Eddy Accumulation; see Zahn and Bou-Zeid 2024), half-hourly transpiration-to-evapotranspiration (T/ET) ratios were derived from 20 hertz (Hz, cycles per second) eddy covariance measurements of carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water vapor (H₂O) concentrations. The dataset spans six vegetation types including evergreen and deciduous forests, grasslands, cultivated crops, shrublands, and emergent herbaceous wetlands.

Data Package Contents: The dataset includes a single CSV (comma-separated values) file containing daily anomalies (deviations from baseline conditions) for transpiration (Delta_T), evaporation (Delta_E), total evapotranspiration (Delta_ET), and T/ET ratio (Delta_T_ET) during each day of identified heatwave events. The file also includes site codes, dates, heatwave event identifiers, and day-of-heatwave indicators. The CSV file can be opened with spreadsheet software (Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets) or programming environments (Python, R, MATLAB).

This resource enables researchers to investigate ecosystem-specific responses to thermal extremes, validate land surface model partitioning of ET fluxes, and examine feedbacks between water cycling and surface energy balance during heatwaves. The dataset is particularly valuable for studies linking vegetation hydraulic strategies to climate resilience, as it captures the divergent responses of shallow-rooted versus deep-rooted ecosystems. Potential applications include improving drought early warning systems, informing irrigation management strategies, and advancing our mechanistic understanding of land-atmosphere interactions under extreme heat conditions.

provider.name: Improving ESS Approaches to Evapotranspiration Partitioning Through Data Fusion

measurementTechnique: A total of 32 NEON terrestrial flux sites across the contiguous United States were selected, representing six vegetation types: Evergreen Forest (8 sites), Deciduous Forest (12 sites), Cultivated Crops (4 sites), Grassland (3 sites), Emergent Herbaceous Wetlands (3 sites), and Shrubland (2 sites). All sites are equipped with CSAT-3 sonic anemometers (Campbell Scientific Inc.) measuring wind speed and direction at 20 Hz, and LI-7200/LI-7200RS infrared gas analyzers (Li-Cor Inc.) monitoring water vapor and CO₂ concentrations at the same frequency.

Heatwave events were defined as sequences of at least three consecutive days during which daily maximum air temperature exceeded the site-specific 90th percentile of the 2019–2021 daily maximum temperature distribution. This approach identified 268 heatwave events across the study period, with durations ranging from 3 to 17 days (mean: 7 days).

Four complementary methods were employed to partition observed ET into soil evaporation (E) and vegetation transpiration (T):
4a. Flux-variance Similarity (FVS) Method: Decomposes high-frequency CO₂ and H₂O time series to distinguish stomatal processes (transpiration, photosynthesis) from non-stomatal processes (soil evaporation, soil respiration) using water use efficiency (WUE) parameterizations. Five WUE estimation approaches were applied and averaged (Scanlon et al., 2019).
4b. Conditional Eddy Covariance (CEC) Method: Selectively samples emissions from soil (high in CO₂ and H₂O) and canopy-interacted emissions (low in CO₂, high in H₂O) using indicator functions. Sample fluxes were calculated only when respective quadrants contained at least 2% of total data points (Zahn et al., 2022, 2024).
4c. Combined CEC and Water-Use Efficiency (CECw) Method: Integrates WUE into the CEC framework, applying the same five WUE parameterization schemes as FVS and averaging results (Zahn et al., 2024).
4d. Conditional Eddy Accumulation (CEA) Method: Expands on CEC by considering both updrafts and downdrafts, isolating turbulent structures originating from soil or plant canopy based on fluctuations in CO₂, H₂O, and vertical wind velocity (Zahn et al., 2022, 2024).

Final T/ET ratios and E/T fluxes were obtained by averaging outputs from all four methods. This ensemble approach mitigates structural biases and random errors inherent in individual algorithms, following best practices in complex system modeling (Tebaldi & Knutti, 2007). Standard deviation among methods serves as a metric of methodological uncertainty.

Daily and half-hourly anomalies were computed relative to a non-heatwave baseline defined as the average value over the 30-day period preceding each heatwave onset. Days meeting heatwave criteria within this window were excluded from baseline calculations. Absolute anomalies (ΔT/ET) and relative anomalies (αT/ET) were calculated for ET, E, T, and T/ET.

More detailed information on methods can be found in: Han Chen, Stephen P. Good, Einara Zahn, Elie Bou-Zeid, Kelly K. Caylor, Richard P. Fiorella, Marja Haagsma, Lixin Wang (2026). Shifts in evapotranspiration components during heatwaves alter surface cooling. Earth's Future, doi: 10.1029/2025EF006562.
